title: Adams County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Adams County wells have a 55 ft median depth and 12 gpm median reported yield. Compare drilling costs, water levels and risks before buying land.
h1: What to Expect from a Well in Adams County
intro_html:
A 55 ft median well depth makes Adams County look like shallow drilling country. That is only part of the picture: the middle half of reported depths runs from 30 to 352 ft. A shallow well near your property does not establish the budget for your lot.

Colorado DWR records include 25,850 permitted wells countywide, with 13,856 recorded as constructed. For a purchase in Brighton, Todd Creek or Henderson, start with nearby completed wells, then check their aquifer, permitted use and construction details.

sections.heading: Why Adams County's Shallow Median Can Mislead
sections.html:
Of the 15,156 wells reporting depth, the median is 55 ft, and 60% are under 100 ft. Yet 21% fall in the 300-600 ft range and 9% are 600+ ft. The 90th-percentile depth is 560 ft. This is not a county where a single depth allowance fits every parcel.

Permits name Alluvial and Upper Arapahoe aquifers, while many leave the aquifer unnamed or use a broad bedrock label. Alluvial deposits and Denver Basin sedimentary formations present different drilling targets. The 30-352 ft middle-half range means a bid should identify the intended aquifer and explain extra-depth charges. Compare construction logs around your lot in Brighton or Henderson rather than pricing from the county median alone.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Are Encouraging, but Test the Well
sections.html:
The 4,286 records with pump yields show a 12.0 gpm median, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gpm. Those rates can support ordinary household demand when the well sustains its output and the pump system is properly sized. Recorded output is not a promise of current performance.

The reported share under 1 gpm is 0%, while 2% fall in the 1-5 gpm range. That gives little indication of widespread very-low-yield performance in the reporting subset, but it does not prove dry holes or weak wells are absent. For an existing home, request a pumping and recovery test. Also check permitted uses: a productive well does not automatically authorize irrigation, livestock watering or additional residences.

sections.heading: Water Levels Do Not Show a Steady Countywide Decline
sections.html:
Static water level is where water stands in an idle well, not the bottom of the drilled hole. Among 1,280 reporting records, the median depth to water is 36 ft, with a middle-half range of 12-120 ft. Pump placement must account for the water level while pumping, not just this resting measurement.

The decade medians fluctuate rather than decline consistently: 30 ft in the 1950s, 85 ft in the 1970s, 170 ft in the 1990s, 33 ft in the 2000s, 70 ft in the 2010s and 33 ft in the 2020s. These are different measurement groups, not a continuous record from the same wells. They do not establish a countywide falling water table or rule out localized declines.

sections.heading: A Long Permit History, Not Just Household Wells
sections.html:
Adams County's permit history extends from 1,001 permits in the 1950s to 4,860 in the 2000s. Records show 3,924 in the 2010s and 2,038 in the still-incomplete 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2026. Do not treat that partial decade as a completed comparison.

The use mix matters when screening neighbors: 39% are domestic/household and 35% are monitoring wells. A nearby monitoring record is not a household performance benchmark.

Named drillers include Crandall Drilling & Pump Service (Crandall Jr., Howard H.), with 1,322 records, and John'S Drilling Inc. (John, Lloyd), with 744. The largest listed entry, Authorized (Pe, Pg), has 4,576 records but is not a clearly identified drilling business. Historical listings do not establish current availability.

sections.heading: Budgeting a New Well in Denver Basin Ground
sections.html:
The supplied Adams County cost model assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock at $50-$70 per foot. At the 55 ft median depth, it estimates about $2,800-$3,800 for the drilled hole and $8,800-$15,800 for a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical.

Use that as a starting allowance, not a parcel-specific quote. The county's broad depth range makes the target formation especially important. A lot requiring deeper drilling will not fit a median-depth budget. Ask the contractor to separate drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, trenching and electrical work. Confirm what happens if the target produces poorly and whether access preparation or unusual site conditions change the price.

sections.heading: Environmental Flags and Site Constraints to Check
sections.html:
The supplied environmental mapping lists 1,344 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 194 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites and 13 historic mine features within about 10 miles. Those counts are screening flags, not evidence that a particular Adams County well is contaminated. Sampling locations and confirmed contamination are not interchangeable.

Before closing, obtain current water testing and use nearby site records to decide whether additional analytes are warranted. Check casing, grout, the well cap and drainage around the wellhead. A reported yield cannot establish drinking-water safety. For a building lot, have the well and septic layout reviewed together, including required separation, replacement space and drilling access. No dry-hole statistic is supplied, so the yield records should not be read as a drilling-success guarantee.

sections.heading: Before Buying a Lot in Todd Creek, Brighton or Henderson
sections.html:
Start with the actual parcel, not a countywide average. Locate nearby constructed domestic wells and compare their depths, aquifers, completion logs and reported yields. Separate those from monitoring wells and permits that never became completed wells. Ask for the existing well's permit, construction report, pump information, recent water test and service history.

For an undeveloped lot in Todd Creek, Brighton or Henderson, confirm the legal water supply with DWR before committing to construction. Household-use restrictions may not cover the outdoor uses you intend, and some proposals require augmentation. Then coordinate the house, septic system, driveway, well location and utility route. Get a written drilling scope tied to nearby logs and a clear plan for poor production or additional depth.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Adams County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 55 ft, but the middle half spans 30-352 ft. That wide spread matters more to a buyer than the median alone. Alluvial and deeper sedimentary aquifer targets can require different construction. Compare nearby completed wells in the intended aquifer before accepting a depth allowance in a drilling bid.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Adams County?
faq.a: The supplied model uses $50-$70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 55 ft median depth, the hole is about $2,800-$3,800, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $8,800-$15,800. A deeper target or difficult site conditions can move the project beyond that median-depth estimate.

faq.q: How much water do Adams County wells produce?
faq.a: Among 4,286 records reporting pump yield, the median is 12.0 gpm and the middle half is 10.0-15.0 gpm. Those figures are useful screening information, not a guarantee for a specific property. Before buying, have the existing well tested for sustained output and recovery, and confirm that its permit allows your intended uses.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Adams County?
faq.a: Countywide well records cannot establish whether an individual supply is safe. Environmental mapping lists 1,344 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 194 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but proximity does not prove contamination. Obtain current water testing, review nearby environmental records and inspect the wellhead, casing and drainage before relying on the supply.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Adams County?
faq.a: The supplied decade medians do not show a steady countywide decline. Median static depth was 170 ft in the 1990s, 33 ft in the 2000s, 70 ft in the 2010s and 33 ft in the 2020s. These groups contain different measurements. Evaluate repeated readings from the property or nearby wells in the same aquifer for a local trend.

Coordinate those plans with the well location and drilling access before breaking ground.
